one_line_contribution: The paper proposes a substitution ratio S measuring how much of an ExpeL-style memory bank's paired accuracy gain over no-memory (cell I0×M1 vs I0×M0) survives once a GEPA-optimized instruction that never saw the bank is substituted in (I1×M1 vs I1×M0), plus a companion claim that a frozen instruction compiled offline from the same bank (cell I0×M2, no retrieval) matches live per-instance retrieval (I0×M1) within 2 points — i.e., that most of what agentic-memory papers currently credit to retrieval is really crediting an unoptimized instruction baseline.
closest_prior_work: MemDelta (arXiv 2606.29914) is correctly identified by the authors as the nearest published work — it shows agent-memory headline gains (Mem0 vs verbatim RAG on LongMemEval-S) reverse under a controlled embedding-model swap, establishing that memory-vs-no-memory comparisons are confounded. It runs no prompt optimizer and makes no compilation prediction, so it is a genus match (confound-auditing), not a claim match, and I accept the authors' own framing there. More concerning is the self-reported, unresolved TERMS-Bench lead: the Preprint Collision Check states a prior-round reviewer flagged a paper called TERMS-Bench, described as 'a GEPA-based substitution test for an architectural intervention in negotiation agents' — which, if real, is structurally almost exactly this proposal's central move (use a prompt optimizer as the control condition for a non-prompt intervention) — and the authors admit they cannot verify it exists. That is the work that actually threatens novelty here, and it is left open, not closed.
strongest_objection: The PRECHECK GATE requires the constructed ExpeL-style bank (M1, top-k=7 retrieval — the same design point this research track's own prior controlled evaluation already tested) to clear a ≥10-point paired accuracy gain over no-memory before S is even computed; a bank that fails is 'enriched... until it passes.' But the track's own established prior result, which proposals are told to treat as their starting position, found that injecting a full retrieved bank at this same design point fixed zero items and broke six to seven (p=0.031, p=0.016, replicated across runs) — net harmful, not a ≥10-point gain. If that finding replicates in this study's own from-scratch bank (plausible, given the near-identical setup), the authors will tune/enrich the bank until an artificial positive effect appears before the substitution question is even asked. That means S would be measured only in the regime where memory has already been made to work, not in the regime this track's own data shows is typical — so a headline 'S ≥ 0.6' would license the claim 'instruction optimization substitutes for memory' only for hand-picked, gate-passing banks, a materially narrower claim than the abstract advertises. A track-savvy reviewer would ask why the harmful/near-zero-gain regime — the modal case in this track's own prior data — is excluded from the central comparison by construction (via the gate) instead of being reported as a first-class outcome in its own right.
what_would_fix_it: Report the pre-enrichment bank's gain, with its fix/break decomposition, as a headline number in its own right rather than only as a pass/fail gate, and pre-register how much enrichment was required to pass — that quantity speaks directly to how representative the 'memory already works' precondition is relative to the harmful/near-zero regime this track has already documented. Reinstate a reduced I2 (instruction optimized with memory in context, even 1-2 seeds) so the study says something about coupling/co-adaptation, since cutting the one condition that tests actual coupling is the most reviewer-visible gap for a track framed around coupling memory with optimization. Resolve the TERMS-Bench question explicitly — confirm it doesn't exist, or state what changes in the novelty claim if it does — before relying on the collision check as established.
missing_baseline: I2 — the optimize-with-memory-in-context / co-adaptation arm — which the authors explicitly cut ('it tests co-adaptation, not substitution, and does not carry the claim'). This research track is specifically about coupling self-editing memory with prompt optimization, including whether the pair overfits to each other under joint evolution and where the two fail on disjoint slices; a reviewer for this track would demand at least a minimal I2 so the paper can say something about the coupled condition, not only about the two components measured in isolation and then subtracted from one another.
preprint_collision: The check is unusually careful for this format: it names specific papers with arXiv IDs, quotes them, explicitly distinguishes 'genus' collision (MemDelta's general 'memory baselines are confounded' thesis) from 'claim' collision, and notably walks back five citations from an earlier draft (ActMem, MAS-PromptBench, TERMS-Bench, MemAPO, 'Evaluating Memory Structure in LLM Agents') that a re-run search could not verify, stating plainly it will not rely on them for novelty. That self-correction is a genuine sign of process rigor, not a weakness by itself. But it leaves a live, self-identified, unresolved threat: TERMS-Bench, described by a prior-round reviewer as 'a GEPA-based substitution test for an architectural intervention in negotiation agents,' is exactly the kind of paper that would gut this proposal's novelty if it exists, and the authors state outright they cannot confirm or deny it. An unverifiable 'closest structural precedent' the authors themselves cannot rule out is not a neutral disclosure — it is an open novelty risk the check surfaces but does not close. The check also admits it could not sweep OpenReview 2026 submissions, where a combined-system paper could contain exactly this ablation in an appendix without surfacing in an arXiv search.
